newsitem.title: UK: IRA plan more attacks but Christmas truce - paper.
newsitem.headline: IRA plan more attacks but Christmas truce - paper.

text.p: IRA guerrillas plan more anti-British attacks but will call a temporary Christmas truce, in a carrot-and-stick move to win a place in peace talks for their political wing, a British newspaper reported on Sunday.

Quoting British and Irish security sources, the Sunday Times said a recent special "convention" of IRA fighters had opted against returning to all-out war and agreed conditions on which it might restore a truce abandoned two years ago.

"The IRA decided ...on a "twin track strategy' of political pressure and occasional spectacular atrocities, aimed at putting maximum pressure on the British government to make concessions to the republican terrorist group," the paper said.
A Christmas truce, which the IRA traditionally operated for around 72 hours during their 1969-1994 war on British security forces, might last for about a month, according to the report.
Police chiefs in London and Belfast recently warned that the guerrillas could launch further strikes in a bombing campaign that restarted in February after a 17-month respite.
"There has been no abandonment of violence and we are aware of preparations for such attacks," a senior Northern Irish police officer was quoted as telling the paper.

"But we do not expect or anticipate widespread violence on the scale of the previous IRA campaign. The clear direction is towards more controlled use of violence and a ceasefire at some stage on the best terms they can get."
Political leaders in London, Dublin and Washington have implored the guerrillas to call off violence to allow their Sinn Fein political arm to take up a seat in peace talks.

The guerrillas, suspicious that Britain will stonewall and keep Sinn Fein from talks, say the province's problems must be resolved in negotiations but reserve what they term their right to wage war against "British intransigence".
Britain and Ireland, sponsoring current multi-party talks in Belfast, are adamant that Sinn Fein will not be admitted without an unequivocal IRA ceasefire.
The Sunday Times, quoting republican and Irish police sources, said the IRA might make a public statement within two weeks on what it would take for it to restore its truce.
The terms, reportedly agreed at a meeting held in a country area in County Mayo western Ireland nine days ago, comprise demands previously made by Sinn Fein leaders.
These include an immediate seat for Sinn Fein in all-party talks, a six-months talks timetable, an end to demands for early IRA disarmament and the release of convicted guerrillas.

On Saturday moderate nationalist leader John Hume urged the IRA to call an immediate truce and said British Prime Minister John Major could pave the way for one by clearly stating his wish for substantial all-party talks with a clear timetable.
Multi-party talks have struggled since June, blighted by wrangling on how to achieve IRA disarmament and other matters.
Pro-British "Unionist" politicians, speaking for the region's majority Protestants, insist IRA guns be handed over to prove any IRA truce is not just a "ceasefire of convenience".
Republicans argue that in-fighting by Unionist parties vying for votes in the run-up to a Spring 1997 British general election underpins Protestant inflexibility on disarmament.
Republicans say the IRA will not call a truce without a signal from London that Unionists will not be allowed to dominate any new all-party talks.
